content: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a spiral-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium that is a known causative agent of various gastric and extra-gastric diseases. It is estimated that more than 50% of the global population is infected with H. pylori, with the infection typically acquired during childhood and persisting throughout life. H. pylori is a major contributor to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric malignancies. In 1994, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified H. pylori as a Group I carcinogen, making it the only bacterium definitively linked to gastric cancer. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have shown that eradicating H. pylori can significantly reduce the recurrence of gastric and duodenal ulcers and, in some cases, lower the risk of gastric cancer, particularly in individuals without precancerous gastric lesions or those who have undergone curative endoscopic mucosal resection for early gastric cancer. H. pylori infection has also been associated with extra-digestive conditions, including urticaria, idiopathic thrombocytopenia, growth retardation, and iron deficiency anemia. While the relationship between H. pylori and some of these conditions remains under investigation, there is evidence supporting its role in idiopathic thrombocytopenia and iron deficiency. Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting approximately two billion people. Severe iron deficiency, defined by hemoglobin levels below 5.0 g/dL, can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, headaches, dizziness, and appetite loss. In children, iron deficiency increases susceptibility to infections and impairs cognitive development, while in pregnant women, it contributes to approximately 40% of maternal deaths in developing countries. Several epidemiological studies have reported an association between H. pylori infection and iron deficiency. For example, a large U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) conducted between 1999 and 2000 found a significant link between H. pylori infection and increased prevalence of iron deficiency. Similar findings have been reported in national health surveys conducted in Denmark, South Korea, and Germany. In Denmark, a study revealed that 22.1% of premenopausal women with H. pylori infection had iron deficiency (serum ferritin < 12 μg/L), compared to 17.5% of uninfected premenopausal women. Additionally, case reports and studies from the late 1990s suggested that eradicating H. pylori could improve refractory iron deficiency anemia, particularly in children and adolescents. Iron supplementation is the standard treatment for iron deficiency and iron deficiency anemia. However, some individuals, especially children and adolescents, exhibit refractory iron deficiency anemia that does not respond to supplementation. In 1993, a case report first described an association between H. pylori-induced antral gastritis and iron deficiency anemia in a patient unresponsive to iron supplementation. Subsequent studies, including a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in pre-adolescent children, demonstrated that H. pylori eradication therapy significantly improved hemoglobin levels. Standard eradication regimens typically involve a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two antibiotics, such as amoxicillin and clarithromycin or a 5-nitroimidazole, administered for one to two weeks. Sequential or quadruple therapy regimens, which include PPI/bismuth and additional antibiotics, are also used. Despite the efficacy of these therapies, adverse effects such as diarrhea and dyspepsia are common, and increasing antimicrobial resistance has reduced eradication success rates. The mechanisms by which H. pylori infection affects iron metabolism are not fully understood, but several hypotheses have been proposed. One theory suggests that H. pylori-induced chronic gastritis alters gastric physiology, impairing dietary iron absorption. Gastric mucosal integrity is essential for optimal iron absorption, and H. pylori infection can lead to hypochlorhydria and reduced ascorbic acid levels in gastric juices, both of which decrease non-heme iron absorption. Additionally, individuals with H. pylori infection may use antacids, which raise gastric pH and further impair iron absorption. Another hypothesis involves the sequestration of iron by H. pylori. Iron is a critical nutrient for the bacterium's survival, and H. pylori produces siderophores that bind heme iron with high affinity, rendering it unavailable for host absorption. Chronic infection also depletes iron stores as part of the immune response to bacterial infection. H. pylori may sense iron concentrations and use them as signals to activate virulence mechanisms. Recent studies suggest that iron deficiency itself can modulate H. pylori virulence and increase the risk of gastric cancer. Furthermore, specific genotypes of H. pylori virulence factors involved in iron acquisition may contribute to iron deficiency in infected individuals. Eradicating H. pylori may improve iron stores by addressing these mechanisms. Evidence from systematic reviews and RCTs supports the role of H. pylori eradication in improving iron deficiency anemia, although some studies have reported conflicting results. For instance, a meta-analysis of five RCTs found no significant relationship between H. pylori eradication and improved iron deficiency. Given the mixed evidence and the publication of new RCTs since the last systematic review, further investigation is warranted to clarify the role of H. pylori eradication in iron metabolism. This review aims to evaluate the latest evidence on the impact of H. pylori eradication on iron stores in individuals with and without iron deficiency anemia.
